name: Loniu
confidence_why: Hamel's 1994 reference grammar, the only full description of Loniu, reports stress as penultimate or final with no rule yet found and no lexical contrast, and Blust's 2021 sketch from his own field materials agrees that stress falls on no fixed syllable and is never contrastive, adding only a penultimate-in-free-form versus final-in-possessed-form pattern for nouns, so the two first-hand sources…
catalog_citation: Hamel, Patricia J. 1994. A grammar and lexicon of Loniu, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics C-103. Canberra: ANU.
catalog_quote: Stress does not appear to be a lexically differential feature in Loniu. It is either penultimate or final, but varies or shifts according to the structure of the phrase or clause in which the word appears. No rules have as yet been discovered for the determination of stress placement. The most that can be said at this point is as follows: (a) Syllable structure does not seem to determine stress placement. The following patterns, marked according to stress placement when the words are spoken in isolation, occur: (66) Penultimate: (C)VCV ['ahi] 'step on'; ['nropo] 'now' ... (67) Final: (C)VCV [E'ku] 'pile up'; [ko'mu] 'word'; [tu'we] 'boil' ... Stress may shift if the words occur in close syntactic or morphological relationship with a following morpheme. ... (c) Stress varies when words are in construction with other words and morphemes in a word, phrase or clause. It may shift and/or …

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the standard reference grammar (Hamel 1994, PL C-103), held in full, and the deciding quotation and domain quotation are verbatim at the stated pages (printed 23-25 = PDF 33-35). Glottolog 5.1 lists no other grammar or phonology of Loniu besides versions of Hamel's work; WALS codes no stress features and cites only Hamel. The one later first-hand source, Blust 2021 (downloaded now, open access via LSPNG), explicitly defers to Hamel on stress, restates that stress 'does not invariably fall on the same syllable' and is never contrastive, and adds an observation that free nominal bases tend to be penultimate while singular possessed forms are final (a historical penult pattern obscured by final-vowel loss). That refines rather than contradicts the 'variable, penultimate-or-final, right edge, not lexically contrastive' coding; at most the the primary-stress rule could add Blust's free-vs-poss

sources.quote: 'Hamel (1994:23ff) deals with stress placement ... and I need not repeat here what she already covers well. Whether stress should be considered phonemic in Loniu remains an open question, as it does not invariably fall on the same syllable, yet never seems to be critical to distinguishing the meanings of morphemes. One pattern that appears repeatedly in my field materials is for stress to be penultimate in the free forms of nominal bases, but final in at least the singular possessed forms, as in [nímɛʔ] 'hand' (free form), [nimóʔ], [nimɛ́m], [nimɛ́n]. This suggests that stress was penultimate

sources.note: Only post-1994 first-hand description of Loniu phonology; p.380 confirms non-contrastive, non-fixed stress and adds a morphological sub-pattern (penultimate in free nominal bases, final in singular possessed forms) worth noting in the primary-stress rule/the secondary-stress rule.
